content: Drug Interactions and Monitoring Recommendations: 1. Ivacaftor and M1 Metabolite: Ivacaftor and its M1 metabolite may inhibit P-glycoprotein (P-gp), potentially leading to a significant increase in systemic exposure to P-gp substrates with a narrow therapeutic index. Close monitoring is advised when co-administering such drugs. 2. Ketoconazole: Ketoconazole can increase the levels or effects of ivermectin by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Careful monitoring is required. 3. Lapatinib: Lapatinib may elevate the levels or effects of ivermectin via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Close monitoring is recommended. 4. Lasmiditan: Lasmiditan significantly increases ivermectin levels through P-glycoprotein inhibition. It is advised to avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. 5. Levoketoconazole: Levoketoconazole can increase ivermectin levels or effects by inhibiting P-glycoprotein. Close monitoring is necessary. 6. Lomitapide: Lomitapide increases ivermectin levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. Consider reducing the dose of ivermectin when used concomitantly. 7. Lonafarnib: Lonafarnib, a weak P-glycoprotein inhibitor, can increase ivermectin levels. Monitor for adverse reactions, especially with P-gp substrates where small concentration changes may lead to severe toxicities. Dose reduction of the P-gp substrate may be necessary. 8. Loratadine: Loratadine may increase ivermectin levels or effects by inhibiting P-glycoprotein. Use caution and monitor closely. 9. Lovastatin: Lovastatin can elevate ivermectin levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Close monitoring is advised. 10. Mavorixafor: Mavorixafor, a P-glycoprotein inhibitor, may increase ivermectin levels. Use caution when co-administering with sensitive P-gp substrates, as even minimal concentration changes can result in serious adverse effects. Close monitoring is required. 11. Nefazodone: Nefazodone increases ivermectin levels or effects by inhibiting P-glycoprotein. Close monitoring is necessary. 12. Nicardipine: Nicardipine may elevate ivermectin levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 13. Nifedipine: Nifedipine decreases ivermectin levels or effects by inducing P-glycoprotein. Close monitoring is recommended. 14. Nilotinib: Nilotinib increases ivermectin levels or effects through P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 15. Phenobarbital: Phenobarbital decreases ivermectin levels or effects by inducing P-glycoprotein. Close monitoring is required. 16. Phenytoin: Phenytoin reduces ivermectin levels or effects via P-glycoprotein induction. Use caution and monitor closely. 17. Ponatinib: Ponatinib increases ivermectin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein. Close monitoring is necessary. 18. Quercetin: Quercetin decreases ivermectin levels or effects by inducing P-glycoprotein. Use caution and monitor closely. 19. Quinidine: Quinidine significantly increases ivermectin levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. 20. Ranolazine: Ranolazine elevates ivermectin levels or effects by inhibiting P-glycoprotein. Close monitoring is advised. 21. Rifampin: Rifampin decreases ivermectin levels or effects by inducing P-glycoprotein. Use caution and monitor closely. 22. Ritonavir: Ritonavir increases ivermectin levels or effects through P-glycoprotein inhibition. Close monitoring is necessary. 23. Sarecycline: Sarecycline elevates ivermectin levels or effects by inhibiting P-glycoprotein. Monitor for toxicities and consider dose reduction of P-gp substrates if adverse reactions occur. 24. Simvastatin: Simvastatin increases ivermectin levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Use caution and monitor closely. 25. Sirolimus: Sirolimus elevates ivermectin levels or effects by inhibiting P-glycoprotein. Close monitoring is recommended. 26. Sotorasib: Sotorasib decreases ivermectin levels or effects by inducing P-glycoprotein. Avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. If unavoidable, refer to the prescribing information for dosage adjustments. 27. St. John’s Wort: St. John’s Wort reduces ivermectin levels or effects by inducing P-glycoprotein. Use caution and monitor closely. 28. Stiripentol: Stiripentol increases ivermectin levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Modify therapy and monitor closely. Consider reducing the dose of P-gp substrates if adverse reactions occur. 29. Tacrolimus: Tacrolimus elevates ivermectin levels or effects by inhibiting P-glycoprotein. Use caution and monitor closely. 30. Tepotinib: Tepotinib significantly increases ivermectin levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. If co-administration is unavoidable, reduce the P-gp substrate dosage as recommended. 31. Tolvaptan: Tolvaptan increases ivermectin levels or effects by inhibiting P-glycoprotein. Close monitoring is required. 32. Trazodone: Trazodone decreases ivermectin levels or effects by inducing P-glycoprotein. Use caution and monitor closely. 33. Tucatinib: Tucatinib elevates ivermectin levels or effects via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Consider reducing the dosage of P-gp substrates where minimal concentration changes may lead to severe toxicities. Monitor closely. 34. Verapamil: Verapamil increases ivermectin levels or effects by inhibiting P-glycoprotein. Use caution and monitor closely. 35. Warfarin: Ivermectin enhances the effects of warfarin through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. Adverse Effects: Common side effects include abdominal pain, asthenia, hypotension, mild EKG changes, peripheral and facial edema, transient tachycardia, dizziness, headache, hyperthermia, insomnia, somnolence, vertigo, pruritus, rash, urticaria, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, eosinophilia, leukopenia, and elevated ALT/AST levels. Rare but serious effects include neurotoxicity (e.g., somnolence, stupor, coma, confusion, disorientation, and death), hypersensitivity reactions, and hepatitis. In patients with onchocerciasis, Mazzotti reactions (e.g., edema, fever, lymphadenopathy, ocular damage, pruritus, rash, and conjunctival hemorrhage) may occur. Special Considerations: Strongyloidiasis: Patients should undergo repeated stool examinations to confirm infection clearance. Ivermectin is effective only against intestinal Strongyloides, not disseminated forms. Onchocerciasis: Treatment does not kill adult Onchocerca volvulus parasites, necessitating repeated follow-up and retreatment. Pregnancy: Ivermectin is classified as pregnancy category C. Limited human data exist, but animal studies suggest potential developmental toxicity at maternally toxic doses. Lactation: Ivermectin enters breast milk in small amounts. The benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for therapy and potential risks to the infant. Immunocompromised Patients: Repeated or suppressive therapy may be required for controlling extraintestinal strongyloidiasis. Pharmacokinetics: Absorption and Distribution: Does not cross the blood-brain barrier. Metabolism: Primarily hepatic (CYP3A4, CYP2D6, CYP2E1). Excretion: Feces (major route); urine (<1%). Half-life: Approximately 18 hours. Usage Instructions for Ivermectin Lotion: Apply to dry hair and scalp, ensuring complete coverage from roots to ends. Leave on for 10 minutes, then rinse with water. Avoid contact with eyes, mouth, or other mucous membranes. This medication is for single use only; discard any unused portion. Storage: Store at room temperature. Do not freeze. Properly discard expired or unused medication.
